newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: World Bank concerned over Slovak '97 fiscal policy.
newsitem.headline: World Bank concerned over Slovak '97 fiscal policy.

text.p: The World Bank (WB) has criticised Slovakia's 1997 fiscal policy, saying the swing from a balanced fiscal budget to a deficit could make it hard to keep its currency stable.
In a report on Slovakia made available to Reuters, the WB said it was concerned that the 1997 fiscal policies could derail the economy from its long-term favourable development.

"Indeed, there are indications of a large deterioration in the general government balance from around zero percent of GDP in 1996 to a deficit of almost three percent of GDP in 1997," the report said.
Earlier this month, parliament approved the 1997 budget with a planned deficit of 36.9 billion crowns, up from the 27 billion crown deficit planned for this year.

"Such a fiscal expansion might undermine the efforts of the central bank (to keep the external and internal stability of the crown), maintain the excessive current account deficit, press real interest rates and complicate the ongoing restructuring of enterprises and banks," it added.
The general government budget comprises the budgets of the central and local governments, the social security funds, extra budgetary funds and other extra-budgetary operations.

The WB recommended the government maintain a balanced general government budget, suggesting it avoid the concession of an excessive increase in pension benefits (planned for 1997), smooth out the implementation of some public investment programmes and allow greater participation of the private sector in infrastructure.

The government's development programmes for next year include 14 billion crowns for motorway construction and multi-billion crown government guarantees for modernisation of the state-run railway system and hydro-construction projects.

The Finance Ministry said that by IMF standards the fiscal deficit would be only some 11.7 billion crowns, or 1.8 percent of forecast GDP, compared with some eight billion crowns, or 1.36 percent of forecast GDP, this year.
The central bank, however, disagrees saying planned bond isuess and loans for government projects should be included in the fiscal deficit.
The NBS said this should total some 25 billion crowns, or 3.7 percent of planned GDP, after a forecast fiscal surplus of 2.5 billion crowns this year.
The central bank has also called for a more cautious approach to government development projects, saying that excessively expansive plans could hurt the stability of the currency.
Slovakia has posted strong economic growth over the past two years, with GDP growing 7.4 percent in 1995 and expected to grow by 6.8-7.0 percent this year.
The inflation rate gradually slowed to 0.4 percent month-on-month in November, putting prices 5.4 percent higher than in November 1995.
